messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Erik was twenty-seven when it happened, walking back to his car after a late shift at the Coast Guard station in Seattle. He had stopped at an ATM near the waterfront, a route he had taken a hundred times. Two men came up behind him—he never saw their faces clearly, only the glint of a knife and the weight of a hand shoving his shoulder. They took his wallet, his phone, his watch, and told him not to look back. He complied. He walked to his car with his hands shaking, drove home, and told his girlfriend he had been robbed. That night he tried to describe it and found there were no words that felt right. He could still see the blade, feel the push, but the story came out flat, as though he were reciting someone else's experience.

Over the following weeks, Erik noticed that his memory of the mugging came in fragments. A flash of the concrete wall beside the ATM. The sound of gravel under a shoe. The cold metal of the car door handle afterward. These pieces did not fit together into a single coherent scene. Sometimes when he tried to tell the story to a coworker at the station, the words would stall and he would fall silent. It was not that he was upset—he felt nothing. Completely numb, as if the man on that sidewalk had been a stranger. This confused him more than the fear would have. He sat in the ready room one morning after a night patrol, staring at his coffee, and realized he could replay the entire event in his head and not feel a thing. It was like watching a movie of a character he did not know.

At work, the Coast Guard routine continued. Erik stood watch, ran drills, checked equipment. But certain moments triggered the fragments without warning. The fluorescent hum of the station's hallway—same pitch as the light above the ATM. The metallic click of a locker closing. Each time, a piece would surface: the edge of the blade, the pressure on his shoulder. They came unbidden, disconnected, and left as quickly as they arrived. He did not tell anyone about them. He did not avoid the ATM or the waterfront—he simply found no language for what was happening. His girlfriend noticed he had grown quieter. When she asked about the robbery, he said, "I'm fine," and believed it, because the numbness felt like being fine.

Months passed. The fragments did not stop, but they became familiar, like a bad radio station he could not turn off. Erik continued his duties without error. No one at the station knew he still saw the knife in his peripheral vision during night watch, or that the cold weight of a life jacket sometimes felt like the hand on his shoulder. What finally brought him to a therapist was a moment of confusion on a training exercise. He was supervising a rescue drill and a crewmate shouted a command—the same tone, the same urgency—and Erik froze. Just for a second. Then he shook it off. But that second stayed with him. He told his girlfriend he wanted to talk to someone, and she found a civilian psychologist who worked with first responders.

In the first session, Erik sat forward on the couch and said, "I don't even know what to say about it. My memory doesn't work right." He wanted to understand why the pieces would not connect, why he could recall the event and feel nothing, why the fragments kept surfacing at odd moments. He was not afraid of the mugging anymore, he explained—he was afraid of his own mind not making sense. And he was worried that next time, the freeze might last longer than a second.
